doc.title: George Wein interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 13, 2001

title: Singing pop songs as a child; mother at the piano
summary: Wein sang Tin Pan Alley songs on kiddie radio shows, accompanied by his mother, and recalls Thelonious Monk playing 'Darkness on the Delta'.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth

blocks.x: I’ll take whatever entrance I can get, believe me. You know I usually introduce somebody as a saxophonist or whatever, and with you I’d have to spend five minutes. So everyone knows your reputation. I want to see if I can take you back a little bit. Music obviously must have been in you from the start. Can you recall as a child what music started to really make an impression on you and where did you hear it?

I go back a long way, Monk. I was born in 1925. And I used to sing the pop songs when I was six and seven years old. I go back to songs, and my mother used to play a little piano and I used to sing songs like “I Want to Go Back to My Little Grass Shack in Kealakekua, Hawaii” and once in a while on a Saturday morning she’d take me down to these kiddie shows where you audition and you’d sing and then get paid. I mean it wasn’t a gig but you’d sing over the radio. That was such a thrill, to sing over the radio when you’re six, seven or eight years old. And I learned all the popular songs. “Darkness on the Delta,” was one of my favorite tunes. And one night I was on tour with Thelonious Monk and he played an encore. He liked to play solo piano encores and he played “Darkness on the Delta.” I had never heard anybody play that tune, “Darkness on the Delta” except when I sang it when I was a kid. And I said, “Thelonious, where did you learn that tune?” People don’t realize that Thelonious came out of that era. And he knew all those songs. It was a great thrill for me to hear Thelonious playing “Darkness on the Delta.”
I suppose he gave it his own unique treatment too.
It wasn’t like I heard it in 1934 or whatever year it was.
Wow that’s neat. And you say the pop songs of the day, these were things that would be like on the radio with vocal groups? © Fiillius Jazz Archive -2-

The tin pan alley songs of the 30s. All these, you know, Bob Hope had “Thanks for the Memories,” all those tunes. I used to sing them all. “Hold Me Honey, Won’t You Hold Me.” You don’t know any of those, because nobody knows those tunes.
But you could go out and buy the sheet music I suppose?

Yes, my mother would buy the sheet music and she could play it. She had to buy the ones she could play. She had a lot of ones she could play because she wasn’t a great piano player but at least she could read a little sheet music and accompany me.
Was your mother — if you said to your mother C7—
No, she didn’t know that at all. She didn’t know anything about that.
No, okay. But she could read the sheet music and so forth. Oh that’s great. So you kind of naturally, you had the piano in the house. Did anybody have to push you into it?
